questions.q: Why is linearity of expectation, E[X+Y] = E[X] + E[Y], so useful for solving brainteasers quickly?
options: It only works when X and Y are independent, which simplifies most problems
It holds even when X and Y are dependent, so you can sum simple individual expectations instead of computing a joint distribution
It is only valid for discrete random variables
It guarantees X and Y have the same variance
questions.explain: Linearity of expectation holds regardless of dependence between X and Y, which is exactly why summing two dice's individual means (3.5 + 3.5 = 7) gives the correct expected sum without needing the joint distribution over 36 outcomes.

questions.q: In the St. Petersburg paradox, why is the expected payoff infinite even though the game feels like it should be worth only a modest entry fee?
options: Because the coin is assumed to be biased toward heads
Because each term in the expectation sum, (1/2)^n times a 2^n payoff, contributes exactly 1, and there are infinitely many terms to sum
Because the game has no well-defined probability distribution
Because the casino always pays out the maximum possible amount
questions.explain: The probability of the game lasting n flips is (1/2)^n, and the payoff is 2^n, so each term contributes (1/2)^n * 2^n = 1; summing infinitely many 1's gives an infinite expectation, even though any real, finite-length trial produces a modest observed payoff.

questions.q: What does the coupon collector formula E[total rolls] = n * H_n (H_n the n-th harmonic number) reflect for collecting all n equally likely outcomes?
options: A single geometric distribution with success probability 1/n
The sum of n separate geometric waiting times, one for each remaining 'new' outcome, each with its own success probability
The expected value of a uniform distribution on {1,...,n}
A fixed constant independent of n
questions.explain: Collecting all n outcomes breaks into n stages, each a geometric wait for a new outcome with success probability k/n and expectation n/k; summing those n expectations gives n * H_n, which for n=6 is about 14.7.

questions.q: For a repeated bet with win probability p=0.6 and even-money net odds (b=1), what does the Kelly criterion f* = p - (1-p)/b say to bet?
options: 100% of the bankroll every round, since the bet has positive expected value
20% of the bankroll every round
60% of the bankroll every round, matching the win probability
0%, since any repeated betting eventually goes to zero
questions.explain: f* = 0.6 - 0.4/1 = 0.2, so Kelly says to bet 20% of the current bankroll each round, which the lesson's simulation shows maximizes the long-run average log-growth rate.

questions.q: Why can betting a larger fraction than the Kelly fraction (e.g. f=0.4 instead of f*=0.2) turn a favorable bet's long-run growth rate negative, even though each individual bet still has positive expected value?
options: It can't — any positive expected-value bet always grows the bankroll in the long run regardless of size
Overbetting increases the variance of outcomes enough that the compounding effect of losses outweighs the per-bet expected gain, shrinking wealth on average over many rounds
The win probability p changes when the bet size changes
Kelly sizing is only a rule of thumb with no mathematical basis in long-run growth
questions.explain: Long-run wealth growth depends on the expected log-return per bet, not the simple expected value per bet; betting too large relative to the edge makes the downside swings large enough that the average log-growth rate turns negative even though each bet's raw expected value is still positive.
